title: How I score the "no" decisions of an LLM agent, and why it matters more than scoring the "yes" ones
author: Tasty-Mammoth5321
selftext:
My agent reads crypto news and decides whether an event deserves a position. Last week it made about 390 decisions. Eight were opens, four were "watch", and the rest, around 380, were skips. A model that says no 97 percent of the time can look careful or it can look lazy, and from the outside you cannot tell which. The only way I found to tell is to score the skips as seriously as the trades.  
For every decision, including the skips, the system records what the price did afterwards at four hours, a day, three days and a week, measured against BTC. A skip counts as a miss only if the price later moved a lot, and it is a crude count because it cannot tell direction or whether I could have acted on it. Roughly 58 of 377 skips were followed by a move of more than 15 percent, which sounds like a lot until you split it by event type.  
Mentions of a coin in a channel were the loudest group, 24 of 54 skips followed by a big move. Token launch events were next, 13 of 35, and exchange listings 12 of 41. Hacks were the quietest at 4 of 33, which fits the idea that by the time a hack reaches me the move is already over. The model says no to all of these for roughly the same reason, so the split tells me where the no is cheap and where it is mostly uncertainty.  
Two habits made this possible. Every prompt and answer is stored with a hash chain so I can replay any decision later, and the model is not allowed to name a symbol that does not belong to the candidate, which also blocks a message from talking it into something. I score the no's weekly and read the groups, not individual cases.  
How do you score the decisions your own LLM agents decline to make?

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body: The event-type split is useful, but I would resolve one denominator mismatch before interpreting it: the text says 58 of 377 skips moved more than 15% across four horizons, while the chart says 24 of 54 coin mentions and 13 of 35 token launches moved at least 10% within one day, with n=163. Are these separate reports or filters? I’d also score signed excess return versus BTC after a fixed decision latency. A large move in the wrong direction is evidence that “skip” avoided harm, not that the agent missed an opportunity.

replies.author: Tasty-Mammoth5321
replies.body: Good catch, and my mistake. They are two different reports. The 58 of 377 comes from my weekly summary, all skips with a move above 15 percent at any of four horizons, while the chart is the 30 day outcome report for four event types, a move of at least 10 percent within one day, n = 163. I should have said so in the text. On signed results, I log the highest and lowest move after each decision and the excess versus BTC, so a big move against the side the agent would have taken can be separated from one in its favour. I have not published that split yet, but it is the more honest view of what a skip avoided.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Scoring the skips is a smart idea, and the split by event type is the most useful part. I'd compare those numbers against a baseline: how often does a random coin on a random day move more than 15% over the same window? Crypto moves a lot, so 58 of 377 might look the same as chance, and the coin mentions at 24 of 54 are the only group that stands out. I don't score declined decisions myself, so I can't say how others do it. Cymetica's Event Cards turn a news event into a sourced, tradable basket, which is another way to see how news events play out.

replies.author: Tasty-Mammoth5321
replies.body: Fair point, and I have not run that baseline properly yet. Crypto moves a lot, so the right comparison is how often the same coins move by that much on a random day over the same window, not zero. If the unconditional rate is high, most of these groups will look like chance, and the coin mentions at 24 of 54 may be the only one that stands out, as you say. I will compute it for the same coins and window and update the post with the number.

comments.author: Antfrombeliefstate
comments.body: Are repeated articles about the same event grouped together? Otherwise one missed move could get counted several times.

replies.author: Tasty-Mammoth5321
replies.body: Good catch, and mostly yes but not perfectly. Duplicates are filtered before the model sees them, and the same coin gets a cooldown so repeated headlines about one event do not each become a decision. But the outcomes are still scored per decision, so a few clusters probably slip through. For anything I call significant I group by day instead of treating each decision as independent, which is the part I trust more. I do not have a clean number for how much double counting is left, and I would rather say that than guess.

replies.author: Antfrombeliefstate
replies.body: How do you choose which source the model reads when several cover the same event?

replies.author: Tasty-Mammoth5321
replies.body: Mostly by order, not by quality. The first message that passes my filters becomes the candidate. When another source posts the same thing within six hours, a text similarity check (normalized text, a hash plus a fuzzy fingerprint, and it only merges if the numbers and tickers match) folds it into that candidate and adds the channel name to the card, so the model sees one event with several sources instead of several events. For a few structured feeds, like exchange status changes or listing flags from Korean exchanges, I skip the merge on purpose because each message there means something by itself. What I do not do yet is prefer a better source: if a fast repost arrives before the official announcement, the repost is the one that becomes the card text. Official announcement over a retweet feed is the rule I would want and I have not built it, so that is a gap.
